**Start from an existing session.** **New session from this one**, on a session's row or tab menu, picks an agent and starts a session in the same working directory that can read the source conversation. **New session from here**, on a message in a conversation, does the same but cuts the source off at that message. The new session shows a **Continues from** divider naming its source; **Open source session** in its menu takes you back.

To fire a preconfigured prompt instead of typing one, open the chevron beside the session composer's **Send** button and pick an Action. Anything you typed rides along as a refinement. See [Actions](/kepler/actions).

***

## Opening a file

Any file can open on the task page, whether or not it's attached to the Task. It opens as a tab with tabs on, or in the **Resources** column with tabs off, in Kepler's file viewer. To see a worktree file alongside its changes instead, pick **Open in Changes** in its tab's menu, which opens it in the Changes overlay on File view. For what happens away from the task page, see [Outside the task page](#outside-the-task-page).

| How to open one | What you get |
|---|---|
| **File › Open File…** (**Cmd/Ctrl+O**) | A file picker for the machine the window is connected to |
| **File › Go to File…** (**Cmd/Ctrl+P**) | Finds a file by name across **This task** or **All tasks**, opens a full path you type, and lists **Recent** files before you type anything. A path that names a folder, or ends in a separator, offers **Open** and opens the folder |
| A file row in the rail's **Files** group | That file |
| A file path an agent writes in the conversation | The file, at the line the agent named. A click or Cmd/Ctrl+click opens it in Kepler, and Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+click opens it in your default editor. |
| A file path in a terminal | The file, at its line. See [File paths are links](#file-paths-are-links) |

**Every file link follows one rule.** A click or a Cmd/Ctrl+click opens the file in Kepler, and a middle-click does the same. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+click opens it in your default editor at its line, or in your default app when that's your pinned target or no editor is installed. If no editor takes it, the file opens in Kepler instead.

A path that's already one of the Task's files opens that file's own tab rather than a second copy, however the path was spelled. A file that isn't attached yet offers **Add to task**, which attaches it and turns the tab into its resource tab in place.

**What the viewer shows**

- **Code and text**, highlighted, scrolled to and marking the line you opened it at. **Wrap lines** toggles soft wrapping.
- **Markdown**, rendered, with a **Preview** / **Source** toggle. A Markdown file opened at a line, such as from a path an agent wrote, opens in **Source** so you see the line, and a toggle you make then applies to that open only.
- **Images and SVG**, fitted to the pane, with **Fit** and **100%**.
- Anything else gets a **No preview for this file** card with the ways out the window allows: **Open in default app**, **Show in Finder** (macOS), **Show in Explorer** (Windows) or **Show in file manager** (Linux), and **Copy path**.

**An open file follows the disk.** When it changes, the viewer updates in place without moving you, and says **Updated just now**, or **Updated just now by** the session that changed it when Kepler saw the edit. **Show changes** shows what changed since the file was first shown; **Back to file** returns. A deleted file keeps showing the last version Kepler read, and says so.

A very large file shows its start first, labeled *Showing the first {shown} of {total}*, with **Load the rest**.

**Open in** on the viewer's header is an icon button that opens the file in your pinned editor, or else the one you used last, with its chevron listing the rest. Your computer's default app is one of the targets, listed as **Default app**, and like any editor it can be pinned as your default with **Set as default**.

### Finding text in a file

Every code view, the file viewer and the diffs in the Changes overlay alike, has its own find bar. Press **Cmd/Ctrl+F** in the view to open it at the top right. It counts matches as *{current} of {total}*, or **No results**, and offers the following:

| Control | Keys |
|---|---|
| Next and previous match | **F3** and **Shift+F3**. Also **Cmd+G** and **Cmd+Shift+G** on macOS |
| **Match case** | **Alt+C**, or **Cmd+Option+C** on macOS |
| **Match whole word** | **Alt+W**, or **Cmd+Option+W** on macOS |
| **Use regular expression** | **Alt+R**, or **Cmd+Option+R** on macOS |

**Escape** closes the bar. In a diff, the search runs across every file in the stack but skips the unchanged lines that are folded away. A file that has only partly loaded says it searched the first part, with **Load the rest**.

Selecting text works across the whole file, not only the lines on screen. Drag or select all and copy, and Kepler loads the rest of the file if it needs to. Double-click selects a word.

### Outside the task page

A file opened anywhere else, such as from the Dashboard or a conversation link outside a Task, opens in an overlay rather than a tab:

- A file or folder inside a worktree opens in the Changes overlay on File view. A changed file lands on **Working changes**; anything else lands on the **All files** tree. A folder opens the **All files** tree with its changed files selected.
- Any other file opens in the file overlay, beside a file tree rooted at the attached folder or worktree that holds it, or else at the file's own folder.

In the file overlay:

- **Show file tree** and **Hide file tree** toggle the tree, and the tree's edge resizes it. On a narrow window the toggle is locked: *Widen the window to show the file tree*.
- **Filter files** narrows the tree. Right-click a tree row for the ways to open it and copy its path.
- The breadcrumb's folders each list their folders and files, plus **Open {folder} in file manager**. As room runs out, folders fold into **More folders**.
- Opening a folder shows its tree with **Pick a file** in the viewer.
- **Add to task** is the last item in **More file actions**.
- Drag either edge of the overlay to widen it, or use **Maximize**.

***

## The terminal drawer

Terminals live in a drawer beneath the content area, spanning all of it, sized by a sash of its own. The **Terminal** control at the right edge of the header shows and hides it, and counts what's running.

| How to open one | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Cmd/Ctrl+J**, or the header's **Terminal** | Shows and hides the drawer |
| **New terminal here**, on a worktree or folder row | A shell in that checkout |
| **Run command here**, on a worktree row | The command you pick, running in that checkout, revealed without taking your focus |
| The strip's **+** | A shell. With several checkouts it becomes **New terminal in…**, listing them by branch |

Every terminal also has a row in the rail's **Terminals** group. Clicking it brings the drawer up on that terminal; clicking the row already showing puts the drawer away. Drag the drawer's tabs to reorder them.

**Maximize terminal pane**, or **Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+J**, takes the whole height; **Restore terminal pane** brings it back.

On a phone, a terminal takes the whole column, with a row of the keys a phone keyboard lacks beneath it, and you select text with a long press. See [Remote Access](/kepler/remote-environments#remote-access-reach-kepler-from-another-device).

### When a terminal reconnects

A terminal reattaches to its running shell rather than starting a new one:

- While it loads it reads **Loading terminal…**. When the connection drops, nothing shows for the first second. After that, a **Reconnecting to the terminal…** strip leaves the last screen readable and scrollable, and only after five seconds does it cover the terminal. If it can't reconnect, **Unable to restore this terminal** says *The terminal is still running. Retry to load its output again.*, with **Retry**.
- What you type while it reconnects is held and sent once the terminal is back. If the program printed something in the meantime, Kepler drops it instead and says **The terminal changed while reconnecting**: *Nothing you typed was sent. Type it again.* Typing that couldn't reach the terminal at all reads **Unable to send what you typed**.
- One view types at a time. A terminal another view is driving, in another window or on a Remote Access device, reads **Another view is controlling this terminal**. **Take control** lets you type here and sizes the terminal to this view.
- A terminal printing faster than the connection can show reads **Showing the latest output**: *This terminal is printing faster than this connection can show, so older lines are skipped.*
- Input Kepler can't confirm is never resent. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#whats-different-in-terminal).

### Reading a tab

Each tab carries **one glyph** that says both what the tab is and how it ended, so a clean finish and a crash don't look alike:

| Kind | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Shell** | A plain terminal you opened |
| **Agent** | A session running an agent in Terminal mode. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs) |
| **Command run** | One of the repository's commands |

A shell tab also shows what its program reports, when the program reports a status: **Running**, **Needs you**, **Done** or **Failed**. Hover the tab to see the state and, from a minute on, how long it's been in it, plus its message, its progress as a bar reading *{percent}% done*, and any sub-tasks with their own ages. A program that's blocked or failed without saying why gets a next step, such as *Approve it in the terminal.* **Reported by {app}** shows only when the app isn't already the tab's name. An agent tab keeps its own glyph, because its session owns its status.

**A shell tab is named after what runs in it.** That's the app, when the program reports its status, or else the job in front, such as `pnpm dev`. On Windows, it can be the window title the program set. Back at the prompt, the tab returns to its own label, such as **Terminal 2**. While the name differs from the label, hovering the tab shows the label and the job's command line or window title. Command runs and agent tabs keep their names.

When a shell's program needs you or finishes, Kepler sends a notification that names the terminal and its Task, such as *Approve it in {terminal}* or *Finished in {terminal}*. Kepler stays quiet while that terminal is on screen in the focused window. These notifications follow the same notification settings as agent sessions, in **Settings → Notifications**.

A finished command run shows a **result bar** rather than leaving you to read the scrollback: **Exited with code {code}**, **Exited by signal {signal}**, or **Stopped**, with **Run again** and **Close** beside it. A still-running one offers **Stop**.

### File paths are links

File paths printed in a terminal are links, including relative paths, paths with a line suffix such as `src/app.ts:42`, and paths wrapped across lines. Kepler also spots a path an agent mentions as `@src/app.ts`, and one glued to a flag, such as `--config=/etc/app.json`. Cmd-click one (Ctrl-click on Windows and Linux) to open the file [on the task page](#opening-a-file) at its line, and Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+click to open it in your default editor. The hover hint says *Click to open*, or *Click to preview* where the click opens a preview tab, and adds *Click to open in editor* when an editor can take the file.

Right-click a path for more: **Open file**, your default editor (opening at the line), **Open in** for the rest of your editors and your computer's **Default app**, **Save as…**, and **Copy path**. Any of those targets can be your default, with **Set as default**.

Kepler task and session links in a terminal are links too, and so are the task and session IDs Kepler recognizes. The hover hint says *Click to open in Kepler*; Cmd/Ctrl-click opens it, and right-click offers **Open in Kepler** and **Copy link**.

On a phone, long-press a path or link instead, then pick **Open** from the small menu over the selection, which also offers **Copy**, **Paste**, and **Select all**. See [Remote Access](/kepler/remote-environments#remote-access-reach-kepler-from-another-device).

### Closing a busy terminal

Closing a terminal with something running in it confirms first, naming the job you actually launched:

> **Close terminal?** *Stops {command}, which is still running in this terminal.*

**Close terminal** goes ahead. A terminal already closing offers only **Force close**.

Shell tabs survive a Kepler update and come back after a restart. With **Keep agents and terminals running across restarts and updates** on, in **Settings → General**, command runs do too, and each takes up its run again: still running with **Stop**, or finished with its result bar. A plain **Quit** ends them, the way quitting any terminal app does. Quitting Kepler counts busy terminals alongside busy sessions and asks before it takes them down.

***

## What each resource pane shows

| Resource | Details |
|---|---|
| **Worktree**, on disk | A strip of verbs (the branch, the sync control, **Open in**, **Run a command**) over its changed files, which lead into the Changes overlay. See [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes) |
| **Worktree**, missing | A metadata card instead: **Current branch**, **Base branch**, and the **Recorded path**, flagged **not on disk** or **gone** when it's been removed outside Kepler. A worktree that has gone stays bound to the Task, and Kepler offers to recreate it rather than quietly dropping it |
| **Folder** | Path, plus an editable name and description |
| **File** | The file itself, in the [file viewer](#opening-a-file), with its description, where it came from, and its size on the viewer's toolbar. **Rename** is in **File actions**, and an uploaded copy says it's a copy in the task folder |
| **Pull request** / **Issue** | Status, who it involves, the item's description and its labels. An issue adds its comments |
| **Link** | Every plain link (one that isn't a pull request or issue) shares one **Links** pane, scrolled to the link you picked |
| **Note** | The note itself, with **Copy note** and **Edit**. The **Prompt** note edits the Task's prompt |

**The worktree strip.** The **⋮** beside the branch, **Worktree actions for {branch}**, and a right-click on the branch both open the worktree's full [row menu](#the-row-menu). With more than one worktree, the branch name also switches between the Task's worktrees. **Detach worktree…** only detaches: *The worktree stays on disk — it’s only removed from this task.* **Delete worktree…** is its own entry, never offered on the repository's main worktree.

**Folders and files.** A name or description you edit saves as you type, and **Done** closes the fields.

**Pull requests and issues.** You can select and copy the description text. When Kepler can't read a description, the pane says where to read it, such as *To read the full description, open it on {provider}.* When the read from the provider fails, the pane says *Unable to read this from {provider}, so its details may be missing.*, with a way to fix it.

A pull request's **People** section shows its author, its **Assignees**, and each reviewer with a badge for their review state, tallied as *{reviewed} of {count} reviewed*. Fold it to just the faces. An issue shows its **Assignee**.

An issue from GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, GitLab Self-Managed, Jira, or Jira Server also shows its discussion under **Comments · {count}**: the latest comments, each with its author, its age, and its text. **Show earlier comments** pages back, and **Refresh comments** reads them again. Kepler shows the comments for you to read; it doesn't hand them to the agent. When it can't read them, the section says why, such as *Sign in to read this issue’s comments.* or *Comments for {provider} issues aren’t available in Kepler yet.*

**Links.** The **Links** pane lists every plain link on the Task with its title and URL, an **Open in browser** button, and **Link actions**. The link you clicked is scrolled into view and flashes.

**Notes.** A note has a name you rename in place: double-click it, press **F2** with the note focused, or pick **Rename note** from its row menu. **Enter** saves the name and **Escape** puts it back. Clearing the name leaves an **Untitled note**. The Prompt note can't be renamed. **Enter** on a focused note opens it for editing. A note with unsaved edits says **Unsaved draft**, and **Edit** reads **Resume draft**. Double-clicking the note's text selects a word.

---

---
# The Agent Graph
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/agent-graph/
product: Kepler
feature: Agent Graph
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Running several agents at once is easy. Knowing what they're all doing is the hard part.

The **Agent Graph** draws it: every task, the sessions inside it, each turn, every tool call, every subagent, and the files the agents touch. It lays all of this out as a graph that updates live, with nodes appearing as the agents work. GitKraken has spent a decade drawing things developers otherwise hold in their heads. The commit graph did it for history, and the Agent Graph does it for agent work.

***

## Open it

The graph is a segment of its own, beside **Todo** and **Tasks in progress**, rather than a way of arranging the list, because it replaces the list instead of laying it out.

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| **The whole fleet** | The top-left control: switch to the **Agent Graph** segment. Kepler remembers your choice across restarts |
| **One session** | The task view's rail carries a per-session toggle on each session row, which docks that one session's graph beside its transcript |

See [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work) for **Todo** and **Tasks in progress**, and for the **List** and **Board** layouts those two segments offer. The Agent Graph has no page of its own, but rather it's a segment of the main list and a pane within the task view.

When opened from the main list, the graph draws exactly what the list normally shows including your search and filter(s). Opened on a session, the graph starts fully expanded and grows downward (or to the right) with the conversation's tool calls and subagents.

The graph is a **visualization**, not a workspace. To work in a session, open the agent session from your Task. The graph's node details link straight through. To watch several agents at once and answer them, shift-click sessions to open them side by side instead; see [The Task View](/kepler/task-view).

***

## How to read it

The graph is layered. Depth grows away from the root.

| Layer | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Task** | The root. One per task. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) |
| **Session** | Each agent session in that task, with its agent and model |
| **Turn** | One exchange: **Turn 1**, **Turn 2**, and so on |
| **Tool call** | What the agent did in that turn |
| **Subagent** | A subagent the agent spawned, with its own tool calls beneath it |
| **File** | The files a call touched: the bottom layer, and where you notice two sessions converging on the same file |

The graph draws only sessions that belong to a task. An external session Kepler observed but no task owns has nowhere to hang from, so the graph leaves it out.

### Past turns start folded

On the main list's graph, each session shows its latest turn open and folds every earlier one, so a long session reads as its current work. A folded card carries a chevron and the number of nodes beneath it, and its tooltip says how many nodes are folded away. Double-click a folded turn to unfold it. Double-click any card with children, such as a session, a turn, or a subagent, to fold what's beneath it again. A session's own graph pane starts with every turn open.

Two node kinds are worth spotting immediately, because nothing moves until you act: **Permission needed** and **Question for you**.

### What a node's state means

| State | What's happening |
|---|---|
| **Running a tool** | Working right now |
| **Waiting on the model** | Thinking |
| **Blocked** | Waiting on you |
| **Finished — unread** | Done, and you haven't looked |
| **Done** | Finished and seen |
| **Stopped** | You interrupted it |
| **Failed** | It errored |
| **Idle** | Nothing in flight |

Three states get a word on the card rather than a colour, because they're asking for something: **New**, **Needs you**, and **Error**.

### Tool calls are coloured by what they do

**Read · Edit · Delete · Move · Search · Execute · Think · Fetch · Switch mode · Other**

This is the fastest read on the graph. A task that's all **Read** is still orienting; a wall of **Edit** means it's committing to an approach.

Repeated calls of the same kind fold into one node badged **Group**, which keeps the kind as its name and reports the count and how many distinct files it spans. That way, a **Read** node reading *9 calls · 4 files* doesn't read as the same file nine times. Double-click a group to unfold it, and double-click again to fold it back up. A single click only selects a node, so inspecting a group never reshuffles the graph.

***

## Click any node for detail

Selecting a node opens details beside the graph. What you see depends on what you clicked:

- **Session**: the agent, state, model, mode, context used, cost, where it's running, and its stop reason.
- **Tool call**: the tool, the exact input, the files and paths it touched, how long it took, and how many calls failed.
- **Subagent**: its type, its prompt, and its own calls.
- **Task**: its status (**Active**, **On hold**, or **Archived**), its sessions, and its resources.
- **File**: a preview of the file. For a large file, the preview reads only its beginning.

A node with children also gets a fold button in the details header, **Collapse what is under this node** or **Expand what is under this node**, which does the same as double-clicking the card. The stats rail keeps counting the whole graph, folded nodes included.

**Duration is only shown when Kepler actually watched the call happen.** Replayed history can't tell you how long something took, so the graph leaves it out rather than estimating.

From the details you can **Open task** or **Open session** to jump into the work, and **Copy** any input or prompt.

***

## The stats rail

A rail down the right-hand side of the graph, reading top to bottom.

It's the fleet's numbers rather than its shape, drawn from the same snapshot the canvas draws, so the two can never disagree. On the dashboard the rail steps aside when you have a panel open.

### The counters

Six tiles, two across, at the top of the rail:

| Counter | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **Working** | Sessions mid-turn with a tool actually executing |
| **Blocked** | Sessions that can't move without you |
| **Thinking** | Sessions mid-turn with nothing executing: waiting on the model |
| **Unread** | Sessions that finished a turn you haven't looked at |
| **Subagents** | Subagents in flight right now |
| **Failed calls** | Tool calls that errored, across the drawn graph |

**Working** and **Thinking** are split on purpose: a fleet that's entirely waiting on the model is a different situation from one that's entirely running commands, and a single "busy" number can't tell you which you have. **Blocked** and **Unread** are the two that should pull you somewhere. Everything else is context.

### Needs attention

Directly under the counters, and only when there's something in it: everything asking for you, most urgent first, tagged **Needs you**, **Error**, or **New**. Each row jumps to its node, which is the point, because at three hundred nodes no per-node marker is findable.

### Throughput

A trace of the fleet's activity over time, and under it:

| Reading | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Tasks** / **Sessions** | How much is drawn |
| **Tools** | Tool calls in flight right now |
| **Files touched** | How many distinct files the drawn graph has reached |
| **Context** | How much context window your sessions have consumed, as a total and a percentage. Only sessions that report usage count, and the row is absent when none do |
| **Cost** | What the work has cost so far, in the currency your sessions agreed on. Absent when they report none, or report several |

### Tool spectrum

The calls broken down by kind, with a bar and a count each: the fastest read on whether the fleet is reading, editing, or executing. Kinds with no calls yet don't appear, and until any do the panel reads **No tool activity yet**.

### Usage windows

Your agent subscription windows, one bar per window per agent, each with the share used. The panel appears once there's something to show. With **Check plan usage with each agent's provider** on, which is the default in **Settings → Agents → Usage limits**, Kepler asks each agent's provider for your usage. With it off, the panel shows only readings your agents report themselves, dimmed once they're out of date, and stays hidden until an agent reports one. See [Settings](/kepler/settings-agents#usage-limits).

The bars here show only how much of each window you've used. Whether you're on pace for a window, and when it runs out at your current rate, shows in a session's usage meter. See [Usage indicators](/kepler/agent-sessions#usage-indicators).

### What was folded away

At the foot of the rail, a note counts what the readability rules removed from the canvas:

- Tool calls grouped.
- Sessions filtered out.
- Sessions Kepler can see but not trace.
- Tasks with no session.

Kepler reports this instead of staying silent, because a graph that quietly hides half the calls reads as "that's all that happened".

***

## Finding things in a busy graph

The graph's header carries a search box, an **Options** menu, the depth slider, and the freeze control. Zooming lives on the canvas itself.

| Control | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| *Filter tasks, sessions, agents…* | Header | Narrows the graph by name, across all three |
| **Layout** | Options | Grow the tree **Left to right** or **Top to bottom** |
| **Zoom to selection** | Options | Frames a picked node with its tree, ancestors, and siblings; holds still when it's already in view. Two nested settings say when the camera may move again: **Follow the tree as it grows** (zooms out as far as it takes rather than stopping once cards get too small to make out) and **Re-frame when the space changes** (reframes when a panel opens beside the graph or the window resizes) |
| **Compact stats** | Options | Same numbers in half the room: circular meters and denser tiles, for a smaller window |
| **Group repeated tool calls** | Options | On by default. Off draws every call as its own node |
| **Only active sessions** | Options | Hide sessions that have ended, while idle ones stay. On by default on the main list, where the **Options** badge counts it once you turn it off, and off by default in a session's own graph pane |
| **Agent** / **Repo** | Options | Narrow to one agent or repository. Not offered on the main list, whose own facets already do it |
| **Detail depth** | Header | How many layers deep the graph draws: up to five, four by default |
| **Zoom in** / **Zoom out** / **Fit to view** | Canvas | Move around. You can also pan by dragging, and press Escape to drop a selection |

Kepler remembers depth and layout per surface, so narrowing the graph on the main list doesn't change what a session pane opens at.

### Freeze it

A live graph moves while you're trying to read it. **Freeze the graph** holds it still so you can inspect a node without it shifting. A chip beside the graph reads **Live** while it's updating (with the moment of the last sample, so "live" is demonstrably live) and **Frozen** until you **Resume live updates**.

***

## What it doesn't show

Worth knowing, so you don't read precision into it that isn't there:

- **No per-turn token counts.** Agents report a context-window total, not tokens in and out per turn. The graph shows context fill and cost instead.
- **No timings for calls it didn't watch.** See above.
- **No cost or latency per subagent.** No agent reports it.
- **External and terminal sessions have no activity branch.** Kepler can see that they exist but not what they're doing, so they draw as leaves with a badge rather than looking idle.
- **Transcripts don't survive a Kepler restart.** A session's history is held in memory for the life of the backend, so a restart empties the branches beneath a session even though the session itself remains.

With nothing running at all, the graph reads **Nothing running yet**, with the hint *Start an agent session and its activity appears here in real time.* Once sessions exist but your filters exclude every one of them, the hint changes to *No sessions match the current filters.*

***

## Early days

The Agent Graph is new, and a lot about it will change. It's worth opening next to the agents you're already running, and we'd like to know whether it actually helps. **Feedback**, in the top bar, opens **Send feedback**:

1. Pick a **Type**: **Feature request**, **Bug report**, or **General feedback**.
2. Write a **Message**.
3. Send it.

Alternatively, share feedback to the public issue board at [github.com/gitkraken/gk-ade/issues](https://github.com/gitkraken/gk-ade/issues).

---

---
# Create a Task
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/create-task/
product: Kepler
feature: Tasks
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Kepler gives you several ways to start work, and the first is usually better: pick something that's already waiting for you.

| Start from | How |
|---|---|
| **Work assigned to you** | Fire an Action on an issue or pull request in the **Todo** segment of [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface). One click, context attached |
| **Something you're describing yourself** | **New task** opens the Task Composer, where you write the prompt and attach what it needs |
| **A conversation you already started** | **Continue an external session**, under the Task Composer, wraps a task around an agent session you began in your own terminal |
| **Another GitKraken app** | A link from GitLens or GitKraken Desktop opens Kepler on the work you were looking at |

***

## From an issue or pull request

This is the shortest path, and the reason Kepler opens on your work. Find the item in **Todo** and click its **Action** button. Kepler then:

1. Creates the Task.
2. Attaches the repository and the item.
3. Sets up a worktree.
4. Starts an agent with the context in place.

Defaults depend on what you're acting on:

- **Plan** for an issue.
- **Address Feedback** for a pull request you authored.
- **Review** for someone else's pull request.

All of these are editable. In the list under the button's chevron, point at an Action to read its prompt. See [Actions](/kepler/actions).

The button rests as a quiet outline and fills in when you point at or select its row. On a narrow card it shrinks to a play icon. On a phone it becomes a single **⋮** menu, **Actions for {title}**, that lists every Action.

Kepler names Tasks automatically from what you started them with. Rename one whenever the name stops fitting: **Rename task** in the **⋮** menu, whose field also has an **Auto-name** button that suggests a name from the Task's prompt and resources. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

<div class="note" markdown="1">

**Nothing in Todo?** Set up your [issue tracker](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations) and [pull request](/kepler/pull-request-integrations) integrations in **Settings** first. Kepler can only populate Todo with work from connected accounts.

</div>

***

## From the Task Composer

Click **New task** or press **Cmd/Ctrl+N**. To start one without switching to Kepler first, press **Shift+Alt+N** to open the quick launcher from anywhere, including when Kepler isn't the focused window.

The Composer is one prompt box above a row of four buttons:

| Control | What it attaches |
|---|---|
| **Add repo or folder** | A repository to work in, or a plain folder |
| **Add issue** → **Issues** | Issues from your connected trackers. With only Linear in the list, a team picker shows every open issue in the team you pick, not just yours |
| **Add PR** → **PRs** | Pull requests from your connected hosts |
| **Add context** | Everything without a button of its own: folders, files, and links |

**Paste a link to attach it.** Paste a pull request or issue URL into the prompt, from a connected host or from Jira or Linear, and it becomes a chip naming the item. The chip attaches the item the same way **Add issue** or **Add PR** would, along with its repository.

In a window connected to another machine, picking a file through **Add context** also offers **Upload from this machine**. Uploads are kept with your draft and saved into the Task's own folder when it starts; if one expired before you pressed **Start**, Kepler names it rather than dropping it silently.

**Repositories and folders come from one ranked list**, not two pickers (*Find a repository or folder…*), and the list learns. Kepler records how often you actually use each place and ranks the picker by it, so the repositories you work in daily are at the top on the day you start using them. The same list is behind the chip's own **Change repository or folder**. Picking a folder that is one of a repository's existing worktrees attaches that worktree itself, and the chip reads **Worktree {branch}**. If the worktree disappears before the Task starts, the chip reads **Worktree not found**; pick the repository again to choose another working copy.

Add as much or as little context as you wish. 

1. Write the prompt: *Describe a task or ask a question…*
2. Attach what it needs, or nothing (which is fine!)
3. Configure each repository (below), if you attached one.
4. Start it.

**The Composer remembers the repositories you last started a Task with** and stages them again the next time you open it. That way, you don't have to re-pick a repository you work in every day. Kepler remembers only the repositories (the branch and worktree settings reset to their defaults), and starting from an issue or a pull request never overwrites the remembered set. Kepler drops a repository that no longer exists rather than staging it.

**It also remembers an unsent draft.** Closing the dialog with a prompt half written keeps it, so reopening picks up where you left off. A Task you have genuinely started writing confirms before it's discarded rather than vanishing on a stray Escape.

**Kepler remembers which repositories you pick for a tracker project too.** Attach a Jira, Linear, or Azure issue and the repositories you chose for that project last time are preselected, marked **Suggested from this tracker project** or **From history** depending on whether the tracker said so or Kepler inferred it from where that project's issues were worked before.

The primary button shows a sending state from the moment you click it, so a slow start doesn't read as a dead button. It fires the Action that matches what you've attached, exactly as it would from a Todo row. A linked pull request resolves to **Address Feedback** or **Review**, depending on who wrote it; a linked issue resolves to **Plan**. With nothing attached, the button reads **Start** and starts the Task with your prompt as written.

The chevron beside the primary button opens the rest: **Prepare**, which creates the session without starting work yet, and every Action that applies to what you've attached. Picking one doesn't fire it here: it relabels the primary button, and an Action that names its own agent puts that agent in the agent pill, so you can check or change what will run before you press the button. To pick one and fire it at once, hold Cmd/Ctrl as you click it. The Action sends its prompt, with anything you typed appended as a refinement.

**Shift+Tab** in the prompt cycles the primary button through the same list. Until you first use it, a hint beside the prompt reads **Shift Tab · Cycle action**.

A Task that has its prompt but no session yet, such as one an agent created for you, says so in a draft session tab: *Start with the task prompt, or describe something else…*. To send the Task's prompt as written, press **Start** on the empty box.

The Task appears in the list as soon as you press **Start**, before its worktrees exist. Until setup finishes, the row carries a **Preparing** pill, and the Task's panel shows its progress. Kep, the Kepler mascot, narrates each stage, such as **Fetching {repo}.**, **Making your worktree.**, **Starting {agent}.**, and **Opening the chat.**, above a list of the launch steps. Where Kep isn't shown, the panel lists the steps under **Getting your task ready** instead, such as *Cloning {repo}…* or *Setting up worktrees…*. **Cancel** stops a launch while a repository is still cloning.

When the new branch is being updated from its base, the session area reads **Preparing branch**: *Updating from the base branch before the session starts.* Then, until the first session is ready, it reads **Starting your session**: *It opens here as soon as it's ready.*

If setup fails, the row's pill reads **Failed** and the panel reads **Unable to start this task**. To change the Task and try again, click **Edit and retry**, or **Dismiss** to clear it. A launch you cancelled reads **Task not started**. If the request itself can't be sent, you see **Failed to start the task**. A Task that starts without some of its repositories warns *Some repositories weren't added: The task started without {repos}.*

If the Task starts but its agent session doesn't, the task page and the Dashboard panel show **{agent} was unable to start**, with **Retry**. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#when-a-session-drops).

### Configuring a repository

Each attached repository gets a chip with three segments:

- **Base branch**: the branch segment of the chip. By default, the Task gets a new branch forked from **the repository's remote default branch**, which is what the chip reads until you pick something: *New branch off origin's default branch, or the current branch if unavailable*. Open it to fork off a different branch instead, to work directly on an existing one, or to take the repository's **current** branch in place.
- **Branch name**: the new branch's own name, suggested from your prompt as you type and editable in place. See below.
- **Isolated worktree**: the worktree segment, a direct on/off toggle rather than a menu. On by default, giving the Task its own working copy: *Runs in its own working copy of the repository*. Turning it off means the Task shares your repository folder: *Uses the repository's own folder, so a branch switch here moves your checkout*. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

**What a newly attached repository starts on is a setting.** These three segments open on **Settings → Tasks → New tasks → Where new tasks make changes**: **Isolated worktree** (the default), **New branch**, or **Current branch**. Changing it changes the starting point only; every segment above still overrides it per repository, per Task. See [Settings](/kepler/settings-tasks#where-new-tasks-make-changes).

Picking **New branch** or **Current branch** means the Task runs in the repository's own checkout rather than an isolated one, so only one Task can use that checkout at a time. If another Task already has it, the chip shows an **Another task is working here** card naming that Task and why, such as *Both would edit the same files.*, with **Create a worktree for this task** to put this one repository in an isolated worktree instead.

### Naming the branch

Kepler names a Task's branch from what the Task is actually about, rather than from the Task's name alone.

- **The name is suggested from your prompt** and appears on the chip as you type: *Suggested from your prompt. Click to edit.* Clicking it opens the field (**Enter keeps, Esc restores the suggestion**), and an edited name reads *Named by you.*
- **An issue identifier leads the name** when the Task came from one, so `KEP-421-fix-the-import-path` rather than a slug with the ticket buried in it.
- **Automatic names are namespaced under `kepler/`.** That way a `git branch` listing in any other tool says where the branch came from, and a hand-made `feat/x` can never collide with one.
- **A name you type is yours verbatim.** The prefix applies to automatic names only, which is how a repository with an enforced `feat/` or `fix/` push rule still works.
- **Your repository's own branch-naming policy is applied** where the host publishes one.

You can set the prefix in two places: **Settings → Tasks → New tasks → Branch prefix** for the app, and per repository in **Settings → Repositories**, on the repository's own page. The repository's page offers **Default ({value})**, **None**, or **Custom**, and shows an example of what a branch will actually look like. Leave the app setting empty for no prefix at all. If a repository already has a branch literally named `kepler`, Kepler says so rather than creating an impossible ref: *This repository has a branch named {branch}, so the {prefix} prefix can't be used here.*

Kepler intentionally forks from the remote by default. If no remote default resolves (no remote, a shallow clone, or no network connection), Kepler falls back to the current HEAD rather than failing the launch.

A repository linked to a pull request always opens in its own isolated working copy, and the toggle is locked: *This repository is linked to a pull request and always opens in its own isolated working copy.* If the pull request's branch already exists on this machine with commits that aren't on the pull request, Kepler leaves that branch alone and starts the Task on a new branch tracking the pull request: *Kept your local branch {branch}*. A pull request from a fork never takes over your own branch of the same name, even one with no extra commits, unless that branch already tracks the fork. Kepler puts the pull request on another name instead: the head branch's name with each `/` turned into `-`, with `-2`, `-3`, and so on added when that name is taken.

Kepler clones a repository you haven't cloned yet when the Task starts, into your **Repositories folder**: *This repository is cloned when you start the task.* Its branch is locked until then (*its branches become available after cloning*) because Kepler doesn't yet know what branches it has, and the chip reads **default branch** in the meantime.

Attaching the same repository twice gives the Task two independent worktrees on it: useful for comparing two approaches, or a mistake if you didn't mean it. Two chips that would resolve to the *same* worktree get a **Duplicate worktree** marker instead, and Kepler creates only one of them. If a chip works in place on a branch another chip has already claimed for an isolated worktree, Kepler marks it **Superseded by a worktree** and skips it; git can't check one branch out in two places.

***

## From a session you already started

You may have begun the work in a terminal before deciding it deserved tracking. Under the Task Composer, and on an empty Tasks list, **Continue an external session** flips the composer to a list of every agent conversation Kepler can see. **Start a new task** flips it back. It's there while external session detection is on.

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Live now** | Sessions live in a terminal right now |
| **Past sessions** | Conversations found on disk, from whenever |
| **Find an external session…** | Searches across both groups |

The list reports what it actually swept, rather than implying it found everything. It says *Showing {shown} of {scanned} sessions, the newest from each agent* when it capped the list, and **Unable to list sessions from {adapters}** when one agent's scan failed but the others didn't.

Picking a conversation carries it on in a new task, reading *Opening in a new task…* while it does:

- A past conversation resumes.
- A live one that's idle in its terminal is taken over, after Kepler warns you to close it in your terminal first so that two clients don't write the same conversation.
- A live one that's mid-turn can't be taken over yet. **Open it read-only** opens it to watch.

### When a task already covers that folder

Kepler checks whether the conversation's working directory already belongs to a task, so you don't end up with two tasks over one folder. It asks under the list rather than in a separate dialog: *{folder} already has a task: {task}*. **Add it to that task** binds the conversation there, and **Make a new task** overrides.

Starting a task from an external session anywhere else, such as from a Kepler link, asks the same question in a dialog:

> **Add to existing task?** *This conversation runs in {path}, which {task} already includes.*

**Add to task** binds the conversation there; **Create a new task** overrides. When several tasks include the folder, the dialog lists each as a card (*includes {path}*), marks the **closest**, and **Add to task** waits until you pick one. Recording the conversation on a task can take a minute, and Kepler says so rather than appearing to hang.

Because a task can be created in any plain folder, a conversation you had in a scratch directory can be adopted just like one in a checkout.

For what happens to the conversation once it's on a task (forking, continuing, and what Kepler will and won't answer on its behalf), see [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

***

## From a folder, or from nothing at all

**A Task doesn't need a repository.** Attach a plain folder from the same ranked picker and the agent works on it in place, with no branch, no worktree, and no Git at all. A folder of notes, a scratch directory, a checkout of something that isn't a repository: all of it is a normal Task.

When you browse for a folder in a window connected to another machine, Kepler opens its own folder picker (turn on **Always use the custom folder picker** in **Settings → General** to use it everywhere). Type a path into its path bar and Kepler checks it before you select it: a folder that doesn't exist, can't be read, or is actually a file is refused with the reason, and a near miss offers **Did you mean** the closest folder.

Or attach nothing. No repository, no folder, no issue. You get somewhere to think (ask a question, explore an idea) and you can attach the real work later, once it's worth tracking. See [The Task View](/kepler/task-view).

***

## From another GitKraken app

You can jump into Kepler from other GitKraken products, such as GitLens and GitKraken Desktop. A link from one of them can open the Task Composer already filled in with the issue, pull request, or repository you were looking at, or open a task or session you already have. A link can also carry a prompt and an Action into the Composer, start a new session on a task you already have, and start right away rather than waiting for you to press **Start**. A link for an item a task already holds says *You already have a task for this item*, with **Open task**. If the repository isn't on this machine, Kepler stages it to be cloned when the task starts. A link Kepler can't fully resolve still opens, with one clear warning about what it couldn't use.

### Which window a link opens in

Kepler sends each link to the window that can use it:

- A link for a task opens in the window already showing that task.
- A link that names a saved remote machine opens in a window on that machine. If none is open, Kepler opens one, and a notice reads **Connecting to {host} to open a link** while it connects.
- Any other link goes to the window you used last.

If a link can't open on the machine it names, it opens on this computer instead, and nothing it asked to start runs on its own. The notice reads **Unable to open on {host}**: *It opened on this computer instead.* When the link asked Kepler to start something, it adds *It was not run automatically.* In a window on a remote machine, a link for something that isn't there reads **Not found on {host}**: *The link may be meant for this computer.*, with **Open on this computer**.

### Opening an agent's own conversation

A session link can name a conversation by the agent's own ID rather than Kepler's: `kepler://session?agent=<agent>&id=<conversation id>&cwd=<folder>`. The `agent` must be one of Kepler's built-in agents, and `cwd` is only a hint about where to look. If a Kepler session already holds that conversation, the link opens it. Otherwise Kepler adds the conversation to a task the way **Continue an external session** does. That needs external session detection: with detection off, the link reads **External sessions are not detected**: *Turn on detection to find that session in its agent.* A link with a required part missing reads **Part of this link is missing**.

***

## After the Task starts

The Task appears in **Tasks in progress** right away, with the **Preparing** pill until its setup finishes. Click it for the side panel, or double-click to open [the task view](/kepler/task-view).

From there you can add more sessions, attach more resources, and review what the agent changed. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions) and [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes).

### Context: what gets handed to the agent

Both paths send the same Action prompt, but they attach different amounts of detail:

| Started from | What the agent receives |
|---|---|
| **A row in Todo** | The full issue or pull request body, attached as shared context |
| **The Task Composer** | A reference (identifier, title, and URL) which the agent fetches the detail from itself |

Either way, Kepler reads each linked issue fresh when the Task launches and saves its description as a note titled *Issue {identifier}: {title}*, headed by the issue's URL. Each note holds up to 8 KB, and all of them together up to 16 KB. A longer description is cut off with a pointer to the URL. Kepler hands these notes to the agent as third-party background, to treat as information rather than as instructions. It frames the Task's prompt as background too, so the agent acts on the messages you send in its session. Pull request descriptions aren't saved this way.

---

---
# Agent Sessions
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/agent-sessions/
product: Kepler
feature: Agent Sessions
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

An **agent session** is one running conversation with a coding agent, anchored to one working directory.

A Task can hold several. Two agents on the same worktree, one agent per worktree, a session for the task folder itself: all of it is normal, and all of it lives under the Task's **Sessions** group. See [The Task View](/kepler/task-view) to learn more.

This page covers the session itself: starting it, directing it, and its lifecycle.

Every session is an agent session, but two things about one vary, and both are properties of the session rather than different kinds of thing:

| | Values | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| **How it runs** | **Chat** or **Terminal** | [How a session runs](#how-a-session-runs) |
| **Where it came from** | Started in Kepler, or found running outside it | [Sessions started outside Kepler](#sessions-started-outside-kepler) |

Everything else on this page (prompts, steering, permissions, status, lifecycle) is the same whichever of those a session happens to be.

For reading what an agent produced, see [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes).

***

## Starting a session

You can start a session from any of the following places:

| From | How |
|---|---|
| A row in **Todo** | Fire an Action. See [Actions](/kepler/actions) |
| The task view rail | **New session** on the **Sessions** group, or **New session here** on a worktree or folder row |
| An open session strip | **+** (**New session**), or **Cmd/Ctrl+T** |
| An existing session | **New session from this one** on its row menu |
| A message in a conversation | **New session from here** on the message's right-click menu |

A quick question that belongs to no task goes to **Ask Kepler** instead, the chat in the top bar's side panel. Any agent that runs in **Chat** can answer there, and **Continue in a new task** hands the chat on to a new task. **Open source session** on that task's session reopens the chat in the panel. See [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler).

### Draft session tabs

**New session** opens a draft tab rather than a menu. Nothing starts until you send the first message, so you can write the prompt, attach files, and pick the agent first. The tab takes its name from the first line of your prompt and is marked **(draft)** when the tab strip has room. In the task rail, the same row reads **Draft**.

To choose where the session runs, open the draft's target picker. It offers the following:

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Search branches and folders** | Filters the list as you type |
| **Attached to this task** | The worktrees and folders already attached to the Task, including **All worktrees and folders**: *Runs in the task folder and has access to all worktrees and folders* |
| **Branches** | Other branches of the Task's repositories. Pick one to start the session on that branch |
| **New branch from this** | Starts the session on a new branch based on the branch you picked |

Every session sees the Task's attached resources regardless of where it runs, so what sets **All worktrees and folders** apart is only its working directory.

A session receives the Task's shared context by default. To start a session that forms its own view instead, untick the **Task context** chip in the draft composer's footer, beside **Attach a file** and the microphone. Its tooltip reads **Leave out the task context** while it's ticked and **Include the task context** while it's not: *Gives the agent the task’s prompt and notes. Later changes reach it with your next message.*

Right-click a draft tab or its rail row for these actions:

- **Discard draft**, which asks first if the draft holds text or attachments: **Discard new session?**
- **Move left** or **Move right**, to reorder the draft among the other tabs.

With **Show tabs on the task page** turned on, the draft's menu is a tab's instead: **Pin tab** or **Unpin tab**, **Keep open** while it's a preview, and **Close tab**, which is its only close. See [Task View](/kepler/task-view#tabs-and-groups).

**New session from this one** starts a sibling session in the same task, worktree, agent, and account, and the new agent can read the source conversation. **New session from here** does the same, but the new agent reads the source only up to and including the message you picked. It's available once that message has finished streaming, and not on a terminal or external session (*This conversation can't be branched at a message.*). **Open source session** on the new session's menu takes you back to where it came from.

**Rename session**, on a session's row menu, gives a session a name of your own. Agents can also name and rename the Chat sessions they start, through Kepler's workspace tools.

***

## Agent, model, mode, and effort

The composer carries an **Agent settings** pill. It holds the same set of questions at launch and mid-session, and its trigger summarizes the current model and mode.

| Choice | Changeable mid-session | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Agent** | No | Fixed once the session exists. Changing agent means a new session |
| **Start in** | No | **Chat** or **Terminal**, for an agent that offers both. Fixed once the session starts. To use the other mode, start a new session. See [How a session runs](#how-a-session-runs) |
| **Model** | Yes | The agent's own catalog. Models are per provider, so a model never moves to another agent. Left at the default, the row reads **Default · {model}**, naming the model the default resolves to |
| **Mode** | Yes | The agent's own permission modes |
| **Effort** | Yes | Reasoning or thinking depth, for agents that offer it |
| Other **Options** | Some | Options an agent can only read at spawn are editable at launch and nowhere else. A Terminal launch offers the CLI's own launch options; see [How a session runs](#how-a-session-runs) |

A change applies from your next message; it never interrupts the turn in flight. Option rows read **Agent decides** until you pick something, **Reset** appears once anything is overridden, and the pill reads **Loading {agent} options…** while Kepler probes an agent it has not seen recently.

When the model a session runs on changes, for example because the default now resolves to a different model, the conversation says so: *Model changed from {from} to {to}.*

Model and mode lists refresh in the background, and again after you upgrade or sign in to an agent, so a newly released model appears without restarting Kepler.

The same menu lists the MCP servers the agent loads for this repository, with **Manage** to change them. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers).

The menu says when it can't offer a normal choice:

| The menu reads | When |
|---|---|
| **Loading your last agent choice…** | Kepler is restoring the agent you used last |
| **Connect an AI agent** | No agent is installed: *Install an agent CLI to start your first session.* Each agent has an **Install** row, with **See all {count} agents in Settings**, and **Installed one yourself?** with **Check again** |
| **Sign in to {agent} to start a session** | The chosen agent is installed but signed out |
| **{agent} didn't share its options** | Kepler couldn't read the agent's models and modes: *You can still start a session. It uses {agent}'s own model and mode.* with **Retry** |

With more than one account, the **Agent** list groups accounts under their agent and ends with **Add another account** and **Install another agent**.

By default, a new task, the Dashboard composer, and a new draft tab start with the agent, model, and mode you last picked. To always start with one agent instead, open **Settings → Tasks → New tasks**, set **Default agent**, and set **New sessions start with** to **Default agent** (*Always the default agent above*) rather than **Last used agent** (*The agent, model and mode you last picked*). **Use default agent** in the launcher picks the default agent for one session. See [Settings](/kepler/settings-tasks#new-tasks).

### Which agents are available

Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Auggie, OpenCode, Grok Build, Pi, and Google Antigravity, plus any custom agent you add. Kepler offers only the agents you actually have installed. See [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations).

***

## Several accounts for one agent

Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Auggie, and Grok Build can each hold more than one signed-in account. Open **Settings → Agents**, expand the agent, and find **Accounts**:

> Run multiple Claude Code logins side by side. Each account keeps its own credentials and history but shares your skills, agents, commands and settings.

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| First row, badged **Default** | The agent's own login, in its normal config directory |
| **Add account** | Adds an isolated account with its own credentials and history |
| **Account name** | Rename a row in place. The name is what you pick from later |
| **Sign in** / **Sign out** | Authenticates or clears that account alone |
| **Check usage** | Reads that account's plan usage. Greyed out only when **Check plan usage with each agent's provider** is turned off in **Settings → Agents → Usage limits**: *To check this account's usage, turn on Check plan usage with each agent's provider in Usage limits.* |
| **Switch account…** | On a signed-in Claude Code account's row menu. Signs that account in with a different Claude login, after a confirmation (**Switch the account for {name}?**) that counts the running sessions using it |
| **Remove account** | Signs the account out and deletes its local data. Your shared skills, agents, and settings are untouched. Sessions whose conversations are stored only in that account are deleted with it; see below |
| Colour swatch | At the left of each added account's row: *Pick a color to tell agents on different accounts apart*. **Rose**, **Amber**, **Lime**, **Cyan**, **Blue**, **Violet**, or **No color**. *The default account stays uncolored*: its picker shows the ⊘ **No color** mark, which doesn't mean the account is off |

An account's colour tints the agent icon on session tabs, the task rail, and the terminal status bar, so sessions on different accounts are told apart at a glance.

**Switch account…** opens the same sign-in as **Add account**. If your browser is already signed in, choose a different account on the sign-in page. On the default row, the confirmation adds *This also changes the account the claude command uses in your own terminals.* When the sign-in completes, Kepler confirms *{name} is now signed in as {login}.*

**An added account can stop sharing your configuration.** An added account links to your own configuration, such as your settings, instructions, skills, agents, commands, plugins, rules, and hooks, rather than copying it. If the agent saves a change to one of these while signed in to that account, the account gets its own copy and stops following yours. Kepler flags this under the account's row: **This account stopped sharing your {items}**. Expand the warning to see which file the account copied, with the paths of **This account's copy** and **Your {item}**, and choose one of the following:

- **Share your {item} again** links the account back to your file, after **Share your {item} with this account again?**: *Its own copy is saved as a backup next to it, so nothing is lost.*
- **Keep its own {item}** keeps the account's copy. **Share your {item} again** then moves to the account's row menu.

**Removing an account counts what it takes with it.** **Remove {name}?** walks through it in steps:

- Running sessions on the account are stopped: *{count} running sessions will be stopped now*.
- Sessions whose conversations are stored only in this account would be deleted: *{count} sessions will be permanently deleted*. To keep them, **Move to CLI account** first under **Keep these conversations**; the sessions stay in their tasks, and removing the account then deletes nothing.
- Otherwise **Continue to remove** asks once more, **Permanently delete {count} sessions?**, and you tick *I understand that {count} sessions in {tasks} will be permanently deleted, and that this can't be undone.* before the account goes.

**How many accounts you can add depends on your GitKraken plan**, and Pro and above are unlimited. A session already running on an account your plan stops covering says so rather than failing silently: *This session runs on a {name} account your plan doesn't cover. Switch it to another account, or upgrade to use this one again.*

### Choosing an account for a session

With two or more accounts signed in, the **Agent** list expands to one row per account, labelled with the account name, so you pick the agent and the account in one click. This is true in the task composer and in a draft session tab.

With one account, the agent keeps a single row, with that account shown beside its name.

A session starts on the account you picked, and you can move it to another signed-in account of the same agent later, keeping the conversation. Session tabs name the account when more than one exists, and a tab whose account has since been removed reads **(account missing)**.

Kepler reads usage figures from the account the session is running on, not from whichever account happens to be first.

#### Moving a session to another account

To move a session to another account, use whichever of these is nearest:

- **Continue as** on the session's row or tab menu.
- The **Account** row in the composer's **Agent settings**: **Restart conversation as** on a live session, or **Resume as** on a dormant one.
- The agent and account part of a Terminal session's status bar.
- **Continue as {login}** on the usage-limit banner. See [When you hit a usage limit](#when-you-hit-a-usage-limit).
- The **Resume** or **Restart** split button on a dormant session, when another account could take the conversation.

Each list shows the agent's other accounts with their login, colour, and usage, and checks the current one. Picking one restarts the agent with this conversation as that account (*Restarts {name} with this conversation as {login}.*), and Kepler confirms **Continued as {login}**. An account that keeps its own history is greyed out as **Separate history**: *This account keeps its own history, so it can't read this conversation. Change that in Settings > Agents.* An account with no login offers **Sign in…**, and the accounts are locked while a turn is running.

***

## Signing in through your browser

Claude Code and Codex both sign in through a browser without dropping you into a terminal. In **Settings → Agents**, click **Sign in** and pick a method: the modal reads **Choose how you want to authenticate.**

| Connection | Claude Code | Codex |
|---|---|---|
| Local | Kepler runs the sign-in, your browser opens, and Kepler shows a status line instead of a terminal | Browser sign-in with your ChatGPT account |
| Remote or SSH | **Sign in with browser**: *Open Claude sign-in in your local browser, then paste the code it returns. Signs in the remote target directly.* | **ChatGPT (device code)**: *Sign in with a one-time code in your browser. Works on any remote.* |

Locally, **Open sign-in in browser** is there if the browser did not open on its own; if the callback cannot complete, Kepler reveals **Paste the code from your browser** with **Paste from clipboard** and **Submit code**. A rejected code says so: *That code was rejected. Copy the full code and try again.* On a remote, Codex shows the link and a **One-time code** to enter there; if your ChatGPT workspace turns device sign-in off, use **Import local Codex login** or an API key instead.

Auggie signs in the same way locally, and on a remote target asks you to paste the JSON it returns. Copilot uses a device code: **Sign in with GitHub**, then enter a one-time code at `github.com/login/device`.

On a remote Codex target you can also **Import local Codex login** to copy your local auth cache to that target. See [Remote Environments](/kepler/remote-environments).

Kepler warns you before a login lapses: *{N} days left before your {agent} login expires. Sign in again to renew it.*

***

## How a session runs

A session runs one of two ways, and the choice is no longer Claude Code's alone.

| Mode | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Chat** | *{agent} built into Kepler, with replies, diffs and plans you can read, review and search.* Kepler drives the agent over the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) and renders the conversation itself. The default |
| **Terminal** | *{agent}'s own command-line app, with its commands, shortcuts and settings, just as you use it today.* It runs in an embedded terminal inside the task |

**Settings → Agents → *your agent* → New sessions start in** sets the default per agent, so Claude Code can default to Chat while Codex defaults to Terminal. To start one session the other way without changing the default, set **Start in** in the draft's **Agent settings**. Where a menu lists agents, such as **New session here** on a rail row, an agent that offers both modes also has a **Start in Terminal** or **Start in Chat** button. An agent that offers only one mode shows no switch at all.

To move a session that already exists, choose **Continue in Terminal** or **Continue in Chat** on its row or tab menu. The session resumes the same conversation in the other mode where the CLI can, and starts fresh where it can't. Kepler confirms **Continued in Terminal** or **Continued in Chat**, or reports **Unable to switch this session**. The item is locked while a turn runs (*This session is mid-turn. Wait for it to finish, or stop it first.*). A session started outside Kepler must be taken over first, and only a session on a task can move to Terminal.

| Agent | Modes |
|---|---|
| Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, Auggie, Grok Build | Chat or Terminal |
| Google Antigravity | Terminal by default. Chat runs Google's separate Antigravity ACP server, once it's installed and you pick **Chat** for the agent |
| Pi | Terminal only. Its CLI doesn't speak ACP |
| Your own agent server | Whichever its command supports |

Kepler works out what terminal mode can offer for an agent from the CLI's own flags rather than from a list of agent names, so a custom agent degrades the same way a built-in one does: a control an agent has no flag for is hidden rather than shown doing nothing.

A Terminal launch offers the options each CLI accepts on its own command line:

| Agent | Launch options in Terminal |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | Effort |
| Codex | Approval mode and reasoning effort |
| GitHub Copilot | **Reasoning effort** and **Model**, besides the context size |
| Auggie | **Reasoning effort**, per model |
| Cursor | Plan or ask mode |
| Grok Build | Permission mode: Default, Accept edits, Auto, Don't ask, or Plan |
| Pi | **Thinking**, from **Off** to **Max** |
| OpenCode | Model and agent, for a new session only; a resumed session keeps its own |

GitHub Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, and Pi also take your first message on the command line when the installed version supports it, so it reaches the CLI as it starts.

### What's different in Terminal

Terminal mode is not a fallback. Kepler wraps the running CLI with the things a bare terminal has no way to give it: the task's shared context, Kepler's workspace tools where the CLI can load them, permission prompts you answer from here, and a transcript that survives a restart. What changes is the middle of the pane.

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| The terminal | The agent's real interface, keys and all |
| The status bar | The session at a glance, then your plan usage. See below |
| The composer | Kepler's own message box, with attachments, voice input, and the agent-settings pill |

The status bar leads with the session and ends with its usage, left to right:

| Part | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Status dot | The session's state and, once it's idle, how long since the model last replied |
| Agent and account | Tinted with the account's colour when it has one, and drawn in a warning tone when the account's limit is spent. Click it for **Restart conversation as** to move the session to another account |
| Model, effort, and mode | What the *running* CLI reports rather than the picks you launched with, so a change made inside the CLI shows here |
| Context ring | The share of the context window in use. Hover for tokens used, available, and total, the estimated cost at API rates, and the prompt cache |
| Branch | The session's branch, with a folder mark when the CLI reports working in a subfolder or outside the worktree. Outside the worktree, the tip's folder line reads **Outside this worktree** |
| Plan usage | Two bars for the **5h** and **7d** windows, coloured by pace. Hover for the full readout; see [Usage indicators](#usage-indicators) |
| **Rich input** | Shows or hides Kepler's message composer. Hide it to type straight into the CLI |
| **No Kepler tools** | Shown when the agent can't use Kepler's workspace tools or inbox in a terminal. Its tip points to **Continue in Chat** on the session menu |
| **Idle detection** | Shown for an agent Kepler doesn't receive hook events from: *Activity is inferred from the terminal going quiet, because Kepler doesn't receive status events from this agent.* |
| Program status | Shown in place of **Idle detection** when the program in the terminal reports its own status. See below |

For an agent that can't tell Kepler it's waiting on you, the status dot's tip adds *{name} doesn't report when it's waiting on you, so check the terminal when it goes quiet.*

Hover any part for its card; a click pins the card open. A narrow bar sheds the least important parts first and brings them back as soon as they fit. Hovering an idle session's status shows its **Last reply**, its **Last prompt**, and, when the prompt cache is about to lapse or has, its **Prompt cache**: an idle session's next prompt can quietly re-read its whole context once the cache expires.

**Idle detection** is a statement about precision. Where an agent reports hook events, Kepler knows when a turn starts and ends. Where it doesn't, Kepler infers the same thing from the terminal going quiet, which is coarser: a long pause mid-turn can read as idle.

Some terminal programs report their own status to Kepler (through the OSC 7501 escape sequence). When the program does, the status bar names that status, with any message and progress the program sends. The hover card leads with the status and how long the program has been in it, shows progress as a bar (*{percent}% done*), and lists any sub-tasks with their own age and message. It adds *Reported by {app}* when the app isn't already the tab's name. When a blocked or failed program gives no reason, the card offers the next step, such as *Approve it in the terminal.* or *No reason given. Check the terminal.* The status drives the session's working, blocked, or done state without hooks:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Running** | The program is working |
| **Needs you** | The program is waiting for you |
| **Needs your approval** | The program is asking for a permission |
| **Needs your answer** | The program asked a question |
| **Needs you to sign in** | The program needs you to sign in |
| **Done** | The program finished its work |
| **Failed** | The program reported an error |
| **Idle** | The program is doing nothing |

If hook events arrive from the same process, the hooks take precedence.

A Terminal session tracked through hooks reports a failed turn too. When a Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, or OpenCode turn fails, for example on a usage limit, a rate limit, or a server error, the session shows **Error** with the CLI's own message once it comes to rest. For a usage limit, that message usually says when the limit resets.

The composer's **Agent settings** pill reports the model, effort, and mode the terminal session is using, but doesn't change them: its tooltip ends *Change these in the terminal*. Change them in the CLI itself; an effort or mode you change there survives the session relaunching.

More differences worth knowing:

- **Paste an image** into a Claude Code or Codex terminal and Kepler hands it to the CLI the way a paste into its own terminal would, so the agent reads it as an image rather than as a path it has to go and open.
- **A terminal session's conversation is recorded**, so quitting Kepler, an idle shutdown, a restart, or a reboot doesn't lose it. Reopening reattaches to the same conversation with its scrollback intact, and the session keeps running through a context compaction.
- **A first message Kepler can't type in safely at launch** waits in the composer as a ready-to-send draft instead: *Your message is ready to send. {name} starts without it, so send it once the terminal is ready.*
- **A first message Kepler can't confirm** isn't silently resent. Kepler holds it, says why, and asks you to *Check the terminal before resending.* The reason reads, for example, *Kepler was unable to read {name}'s version, so it can't confirm {name} is ready.* or *The message was too long to pass to {name} at startup.*
- **Lost keystrokes are never resent.** If Kepler can't tell whether your last keystrokes reached the terminal, it warns *Your last keystrokes may not have arrived* and asks you to *Check what the terminal shows before you go on.* Kepler never resends or late-sends that input. Typing resumes on its own once the input in flight settles.
- **A terminal reattaches rather than restarting.** While it loads it reads **Loading terminal…**. A short reconnect shows nothing; after a second a **Reconnecting to the terminal…** strip appears and leaves the last screen readable and scrollable, and only after five seconds does a cover hide the terminal. If it can't reconnect, **Unable to restore this terminal** says *The terminal is still running. Retry to load its output again.*, with **Retry**.
- **What you type during a reconnect is held**, and sent once the terminal is back. If the program printed in the meantime, Kepler drops it rather than typing into a changed screen: **The terminal changed while reconnecting**, *Nothing you typed was sent. Type it again.* Typing that never could be sent reads **Unable to send what you typed**.
- **One view types at a time.** A terminal another view is driving, in another window or on a Remote Access device, reads **Another view is controlling this terminal**: **Take control** to type here and size the terminal to this view.
- **Fast output is trimmed, not queued.** A terminal printing faster than the connection can show reads **Showing the latest output**: *This terminal is printing faster than this connection can show, so older lines are skipped.*

<div class="note" markdown="1">

**A terminal session is not the same as a terminal.** A terminal session runs an *agent*, lives in the **Sessions** column, and carries the task's context. A plain terminal runs your shell, lives in the drawer beneath the columns, and carries none. See [The Task View](/kepler/task-view#the-terminal-drawer).

</div>

***

## Sessions started outside Kepler

Not every conversation starts here. You run `claude` in a terminal, or you come back to something a week later from a transcript still sitting on disk. Kepler finds both and treats them as what they are: agent sessions it didn't start.

Nothing is taken over without you asking. Kepler binds a conversation to a task; it doesn't seize the terminal that's running it.

### Turning detection on

**Settings → Integrations → Your terminal → Show sessions started outside Kepler** is the one switch, and it is **on out of the box**.

It installs GitKraken hooks so the agent's own command-line interface reports what it's doing back to Kepler. One switch covers every agent Kepler can track this way: **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **Cursor**, **GitHub Copilot**, **OpenCode**, **Auggie**, **Grok Build**, and **Pi**. Google Antigravity isn't tracked through hooks. Turning the switch off silences all of them.

The same hooks are how Kepler follows a **Terminal** session. If a live session's hook events stop arriving, Kepler warns you rather than letting status and notifications drift: **Agent sessions aren't reporting to Kepler**, *Session status and notifications may be out of date. Repair reinstalls the reporting configuration.* After **Repair**, restart any session that still doesn't report. A window that only views sessions running on another computer gets the warning without **Repair**: *To repair reporting, use Kepler on the computer running these sessions.*

Detection is what makes a *live* outside session visible. **Past** sessions are read from the transcripts the agent already writes to disk, so a conversation from before you turned detection on can still be found. Kepler just had no way to watch it while it ran.
