When you open an issue in a reader, either the task panel's side pane or the issue's pane on the task page, a **Comments** section under the summary shows its discussion. Kepler reads comments for **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Jira**, and **Jira Server / Data Center**, through the same connection it reads the issue with. For other providers the section says comments for that provider aren't available in Kepler yet.

Kepler reads up to the newest 100 comments, shows the latest ones with the newest at the bottom, and offers **Show earlier comments** for the rest it read. **Refresh comments** reads the discussion again. Each comment shows its author, when it was posted, and its body as Markdown. Comments are for you to read: Kepler shows them in the reader but doesn't attach them to the task or hand them to the agent.

### Which issues Kepler lists

Kepler lists open work. An issue that's finished or cancelled in its tracker (a Linear issue in *Done* or *Canceled*, for example) drops out of **Todo** and the issue pickers. An issue already attached to a task keeps showing on that task with its real state, finished or not.

**Todo** shows the issues related to you on each connected integration, across every organization you belong to. Providers answer different questions about you, so what counts as related differs:

| Provider | Issues Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or mentioning you |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Yours or assigned to you |
| **Jira**, **Jira Server / Data Center**, **Linear**, **Trello** | Assigned to you |

An issue that's there only because you were mentioned is marked **Mentioned**, so you can tell it apart from work that's yours. Hover the **Related to me** chip in Todo's header to see the rule for each integration you have connected.

To browse beyond that, use **All visible** in the issue list of **Add resources**. For GitHub and Azure DevOps it reads every issue across your organizations, including repositories you can read outside them, such as ones you're an outside collaborator on, and it loads more slowly. Jira and Linear show only your issues there until you pick a project or a team:

- **Jira**: when the issue list shows Jira alone, a project picker appears, starting with **All projects**. Pick a project to see every open issue in it. Kepler remembers the pick for each Jira connection.
- **Linear**: when the issue list shows Linear alone, a team picker appears. Pick a team to see every open issue in it, whoever it's assigned to.

***

## Where your issues turn up

Your issues turn up in three places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | The **Todo** segment lists your issues across every connected tracker, grouped and filtered how you like |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button on a row hands the issue to an agent with its context attached. Firing an Action on an untracked issue is also how it becomes a task |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | An issue is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

The **Issue type**, **Label**, **Project**, and **Status** filters carry your provider's own vocabulary rather than a Kepler translation of it. Azure DevOps and Jira issues also filter by **Iteration** and **Sprint**, each named the way its tracker names it.

Kepler recognizes an issue from its URL when you paste or attach one, including these work item URLs:

- **GitLab** work items, at `/-/work_items/<number>` in a project. Kepler stores them as issues of that project. A group-level work item belongs to no repository, so it stays a plain URL.
- **Azure DevOps** work items, at `/<organization>/<project>/_workitems/edit/<number>` or at the organization level, `/<organization>/_workitems/edit/<number>`.

**Search by key or link.** In the issue list of **Add resources**, type a Jira or Linear issue key, such as `OPS-42`, or paste a Jira Cloud, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, or Azure DevOps work item link. Kepler looks that issue up directly from its tracker, whatever its state, rather than only filtering the rows already loaded. A Jira Server / Data Center link resolves when it points at an installation you have connected.

**Pick from the list with the keyboard.** The issue list in **Add resources** has a preview pane and keyboard picking: arrows move between rows, **Space** selects, and **Enter** or a double-click adds. See [Picking issues and pull requests](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#picking-issues-and-pull-requests).

**Paste a link on the Links tab.** An issue URL pasted on the **Links** tab of **Add resources** is looked up and added as that issue, with **Add as plain link** to keep it a plain link. See [Pasting an issue link](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#pasting-an-issue-link).

**Paste a link into a prompt.** Paste an issue or pull request URL into a session's or a new task's composer and it becomes a link chip, which Kepler attaches to the task when you send. See [Sending a prompt](/kepler/agent-sessions#sending-a-prompt).

---

---
# Pull Request Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/pull-request-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Pull Request Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Connect a Git host and the pull requests you authored, plus the ones waiting on your review, show up in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface). Kepler also matches them to the worktrees you already have, so a branch you are working on carries its pull request wherever you see it.

Manage providers in **Settings → Integrations**, in the **Issues and pull requests** section.

Each connected Git host carries a visibility line under its row, which reads **Everything visible** or how many items you've hidden. Click **Choose what's visible…** to leave organizations or repositories out of Todo, the lists, and the pickers. See [Choose what Kepler brings in](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#choose-what-kepler-brings-in).

***

## Hosts Kepler can read pull requests from

Eight of Kepler's twelve providers return pull requests:

| Provider | Also returns issues |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Yes |
| **GitHub Enterprise** | Yes |
| **GitLab** | Yes |
| **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps Server** | Yes |
| **Bitbucket** | No |
| **Bitbucket Data Center** | No |

Jira, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, and Trello are the other four. They return issues only. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

Self-hosted instances are supported. **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** read pull requests and merge requests the same way their cloud counterparts do, and two servers of the same kind stay separate; which fields come back depends on your server's version. You connect a self-hosted instance inside Kepler with its address and a personal access token, and Kepler checks the token against the server from your machine (see [Connect a Git host](#connect-a-git-host)). The instance must be reachable both from your machine and from gitkraken.dev, so a server that's only reachable inside your network or VPN can't be connected.  Kepler trusts the certificates in your operating system's certificate store, so a server signed by your company's own certificate authority works without extra setup.

GitLab merge requests appear as pull requests throughout Kepler. There is one list, not two.

***

## Connect a Git host

Connecting a cloud Git host (**GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Bitbucket**, or **Azure DevOps**) takes four steps:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler in the browser window that opens.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge in **Issues and pull requests**.

Your GitKraken account holds integrations, not this copy of Kepler, so a provider you connect here also becomes available to the `gk` command-line interface (CLI) and GitKraken Desktop. You need to sign in to a GitKraken account to manage them.

**Connect** hands the authorization for a cloud host to GitKraken's website. Kepler opens `/connect` there in your system browser, names the provider, and includes a redirect back into Kepler. When you return, Kepler refetches your providers instead of reusing its cached list.

While you authorize, Kepler keeps a **Connect {provider} in your browser** dialog open, with the provider's name in place of {provider}. If your browser didn't open, copy the **Connection link** from the dialog and open it in a browser yourself. **Try again** makes a fresh link, since each link works once. The dialog closes by itself as soon as the new connection appears, and Kepler checks for it again whenever you come back to a Kepler window. If Kepler can't start the connection, the dialog reads **Unable to connect {provider}** and says why. **Reconnect** runs through the same dialog.

### Connect a self-hosted instance

**GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** connect inside Kepler with a personal access token rather than through the browser:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**. The **Connect {name}** dialog opens.
3. In **Server URL**, enter the server's address, including the port and installation path when your server uses them.
4. In **Personal access token**, paste a token with access to the repositories you need.
5. Click **Save connection**.

Kepler accepts only an `http` or `https` address without credentials, a query, or a fragment. It checks the token against the server from your machine, keeps it in a protected credential store on this device, and syncs the connection to your GitKraken account. The dialog reports how the check went:

| Message | What it means |
|---|---|
| *Credentials verified with the server.* | The server accepted the token |
| *Credentials saved. Unable to verify the server certificate. Check its TLS configuration.* | Kepler saved the token but couldn't verify the server's certificate |
| *Credentials saved without verification. Unable to reach the server.* | Kepler saved the token without checking it |
| *The server refused this token. Check its value and permissions.* | Fix the token and save again |

Until the upload to your account lands, the provider's row shows **Cloud sync pending**, and you can't make that connection the primary. If Kepler can't reach GitKraken, it retries when you refresh your providers. **Reconnect** on a self-hosted provider opens the same dialog, so you can replace an expired or rejected token there.

Three controls sit on a connected provider's row:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reconnect** | Re-runs authorization. Use it when a sign-in has expired |
| **Disconnect** | Removes the provider (see below) |
| **Refresh** | At the top of the section, re-checks every provider |

A row marked **Sign-in expired** needs its token refreshed. Kepler tries to do that itself; **Reconnect** is the manual fix. A row marked **Cannot connect to server** is different: the integration is still connected, but Kepler couldn't reach the server, so check that it's up and reachable from your network or VPN rather than reconnecting. When one organization refuses Kepler's access, such as a GitHub organization that restricts OAuth apps, Kepler names it under the row and leaves only its items out. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations) for the warnings in full.

***

## Cloning a repository you don't have

Starting work on a pull request whose repository you have never cloned makes Kepler clone that repository first, into your **Default Repositories Folder**. That clone authenticates with the provider token your connected GitKraken account already holds, the same connection the pull request itself came through. As a result, a private repository clones without you having to set up a git credential helper. Kepler authenticates the clone differently depending on the host:

| Host | How the clone authenticates |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Your connected account's token |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Your connected account's token |
| **Bitbucket**, **Bitbucket Data Center**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Falls through to your own git credentials |

For an enterprise or self-managed host, Kepler matches the clone's host against the domain stored on your connection, so the repository clones through the account connected to that instance rather than through a cloud account of the same family. When a provider has more than one account, the clone follows the same choice your reads follow: **Read from this account** where you set one, otherwise the primary.

Kepler hands the token to that one git process and nothing more. Kepler does not write it into the clone's `.git/config`, does not add it to the remote's URL, and never exposes it to the interface.

Where Kepler holds no usable token for the host, the clone falls back to your own git credential helper. Kepler never lets git open an interactive prompt, so when no credential helper is available, the clone fails with a message that names the host and tells you what to do: *git has no saved credentials for this remote and Kepler cannot prompt for them. Sign in with a git credential helper (e.g. `gh auth login`, or the macOS keychain helper) or use an SSH url, then try again.*

***

## More than one account of the same provider

You can connect several accounts of the same provider. When a provider has two or more, an **Accounts** list appears under its row with one entry per account.

Each entry carries two independent controls:

| Control | What it changes | How far it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Read from this account** | Which account Kepler reads this provider's pull requests and issues from | Kepler only, and non-destructive |
| **Set as primary** / **Primary** | The provider's primary account | Everywhere: other Kepler windows, the `gk` CLI, and GitKraken Desktop |

**Browsing a secondary account does not change your primary.** Selecting **Read from this account** on a second account switches what Kepler shows you and leaves the primary alone. The primary is the default read account, so a provider with no override reads through it.

Switching either one clears that provider's saved filters (a repository from the old account need not exist on the new one) and re-fetches the list.

***

## Disconnect a provider

Click **Disconnect** on the provider's row in **Settings → Integrations** and confirm.

Disconnecting reaches further than Kepler: it removes the connection from your GitKraken account, so the `gk` CLI and GitKraken Desktop lose it too. What happens to the provider depends on whether you have another account connected:

- **With another account connected**, Kepler promotes it to primary and the provider stays connected under it. Nothing else changes.
- **With no other account connected**, the provider is removed entirely. Kepler drops its saved filters and its rows from your lists, so nothing lingers behind pointing at a provider you no longer have.

You can reconnect at any time.

***

## Bitbucket has no issues

Kepler keeps two separate lists of what each provider can return. Bitbucket and Bitbucket Data Center are on the pull-request list only, so Kepler never asks them for issues, and a provider filter for issues never offers them. In the list, Kepler builds facets from the rows actually loaded, so a facet with nothing to offer never appears.

The same rule runs the other way for Jira, Linear, and Trello, which have no pull requests.

***

## How pull requests attach to worktrees

Kepler matches a pull request to a worktree by **branch**, and it tries the worktree's **upstream branch** as well as its local one.

That second pass matters when the two names differ. If your local branch is `fix-login` but it tracks `origin/justin/fix-login`, matching on the local name alone finds nothing. The pull request's head branch is the upstream name. Kepler runs a second pass against the short branch of the tracking ref and catches it.

Matching runs against open and closed pull requests together, so a merged pull request still shows on the branch it merged from.

### Confirmed against inferred

Every link Kepler shows records **how** it was made, so you can tell a hard link from a guess:

| How the link was made | Reads as | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Recorded on the task | Confirmed | The link is authoritative. Kepler records one when you launch the task from the pull request, when an agent opens a pull request, when you attach one yourself, or through the branch auto-attach below |
| The pull request's head branch matched the worktree's local branch | Confirmed | A direct branch match |
| The head branch matched the worktree branch's **upstream** branch | Confirmed, and marked | Git-native rather than a guess, but the local name differs, so Kepler labels it **Matched from upstream branch** |
| An identifier parsed out of the branch name | Inferred | A heuristic. Issues only: pull requests are never linked this way |

A confirmed link carries no extra marking. Kepler underlines with a dotted line any link it wants you to look twice at, and its tooltip says why: **Matched from upstream branch**, or **Matched from branch name** for an inferred issue link.

When Kepler finds one pull request more than one way, the most authoritative wins: the task's own recorded link, then a local branch match, then an upstream branch match.

Kepler scopes branch matching to each item's own repository, so two repositories with a branch of the same name do not borrow each other's pull requests.

### Auto-attaching a matched pull request

A pull request you open outside Kepler (from a terminal `gh`, from GitKraken, from the web) doesn't stay a read-time match. Kepler records it on the task for you.

Whenever fresh pull-request data arrives, Kepler looks over your active tasks that hold no pull request yet and attaches one whose head branch matches a worktree's branch. It then behaves like a pull request you attached yourself: it sits in the task's resources, and it reaches the agent as context. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

Auto-attaching is deliberately stricter than the matching above, because Kepler saves an attached resource and sends it to an agent, where a read-time match only draws a card. Auto-attach follows five rules:

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Exact matches only | The pull request's head branch has to be the worktree's own branch name, and its repository has to match a remote exactly. The upstream-branch pass and the rename-tolerant fallback still draw the card; neither attaches |
| Open pull requests only | A merged pull request cannot claim a branch name that gets reused later |
| The head branch has to live in the same repository | Branch matching keys on the head branch name, and the author of a fork picks that name freely. An attached resource reaches your agent, so a stranger's pull request must not claim your branch |
| One pull request per task per pass | A task drops out of the next pass as soon as it holds one |
| A pull request another active task already holds is left alone | One active task per pull request, without taking it off the task that has it |

Auto-attach never archives anything and never replaces anything. A branch match is a guess, so it never supersedes work you started deliberately, and it never removes a link because a pull request briefly dropped out of a read.

***

## What Kepler reads from a pull request

Kepler pulls these fields from a pull request:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Number and title** | |
| **Description** | The pull request body |
| **State** | Kepler derives one of **Open**, **Draft**, **Merged**, or **Closed** |
| **Repository** | Name, owner, and host |
| **Author** | When the provider reports one. Kepler also tracks whether you authored it, which is what splits **Yours** from **Review** on a row |
| **Head and base branch** | When the provider reports them. These drive branch matching and the branch a task starts from |
| **Fork** | Whether the head branch lives on a fork, and where, so Kepler can fetch it from the fork remote instead of `origin` |
| **Created at** | |
| **URL** | Used by the open control, which names the provider: **Open on GitHub**, **Open on Bitbucket**, and so on |

A merged pull request keeps its description and author for as long as a task, archived or not, still links it.

On a self-hosted server (GitHub Enterprise, GitLab Self-Hosted, Azure DevOps Server, or Bitbucket Data Center), images embedded in a pull request's description stay blocked and don't display in Kepler's previews. The server's member avatars still load.

Azure DevOps reports pull requests without a usable number, so Kepler identifies them by URL instead. You should not see a difference; identifying by URL is why a pull request you look up by link resolves correctly there.

***

## Where your pull requests turn up

Your pull requests turn up in four places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | The **Todo** segment lists the pull requests related to you on each connected host, with your role on each |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button hands the pull request to an agent. **Review** and **Address Feedback** are the two built-in Actions aimed at pull requests, and Kepler picks between them by who authored it |
| [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes) | Reading the diff and the commits behind a pull request |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | A pull request is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

**Todo's scope differs by host.** Each provider answers a different set of questions about you, so Todo lists a different set of pull requests from each:

| Host | Pull requests Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or ones you review |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server**, **Bitbucket Data Center** | Yours or awaiting your review |
| **Bitbucket** | Yours, or awaiting your review in your workspaces and repositories added to Kepler |

Hover the **Related to me** chip in Todo's header to see the rule for each integration you have connected. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#which-issues-kepler-lists) for the issue side.

**Review requests come from every host.** Pull requests waiting on your review show up from Azure DevOps, Azure DevOps Server, and Bitbucket Data Center as well as GitHub and GitLab. Bitbucket Cloud has no account-wide way to ask for them, so Kepler reads review requests repository by repository, starting with the repositories you have in Kepler and then the rest of your workspaces at a pace that stays inside Bitbucket's hourly request limits. On a large workspace they can take a while to appear.

**Kepler loads what you're looking at.** Pull request and issue lists refresh while they're on screen, and again when you come back to the window, rather than downloading your whole account's lists in the background. A task's own pull requests refresh when an agent ends a turn, a branch is pushed, or a pull request is published. When one provider fails to load, the others keep loading, and the failed provider's last loaded pull requests stay in the list.

**A failing provider is named, with its fix.** When a connected provider's read fails, Todo, the **Add resources** lists, and a link preview show a warning that names the provider and what went wrong, such as *GitHub needs you to sign in again, so its work may be missing.* On Todo the warning sits under **Unable to load your work**. Each warning offers one fix:

| What went wrong | The fix offered |
|---|---|
| The sign-in needs renewing | **Reconnect**, or **Reconnect in settings** for a self-hosted provider, which needs a new token |
| The provider refused part of the request, so some organizations or repositories may be missing | **Open settings** |
| Rate limiting, an unreachable server, an unreadable answer, or a temporary problem | **Retry** |

Rows kept from the last good load carry a cloud mark on their provider chip, labeled *Not refreshed: shown from the last successful {provider} load.*

**The pull request picker says why its list is empty.** When you attach a pull request from **Add resources**, the picker explains an empty list instead of showing *No matches*:

- If the **Linked work** filter hides pull requests, the picker says how many it hides and which filter hides them, and offers **Show all**.
- If no connected provider can list pull requests, the picker reads **Connect your code host** and lists the providers that can fill the tab, each with **Connect**.

The **Linked work** filter defaults to **No active task**. A task counts as active until you archive it, so Done and on-hold tasks count. The filter has five options:

| Option | Shows pull requests |
|---|---|
| **Any** | Whatever their task history |
| **No active task** | With no task, or with archived tasks only. This default keeps earlier work findable, so you don't duplicate it |
| **No tasks ever** | Never linked to a task |
| **Has an active task** | Linked to at least one task that isn't archived |
| **Archived tasks only** | Linked only to archived tasks |

A row with task history carries a badge: **Task** or **{count} tasks** when one of them is active, **Archived task** or **{count} archived tasks** when all are archived.

When nothing you have connected can list issues or pull requests, **Add resources** opens on a connect view, **Connect where your work lives**, with a tile for each provider. Connect each one you use, then click **Continue**. The provider filter's menu also offers **Connect another provider…**, which opens the same view with a **Back** button.

You can also start work on a pull request from GitLens or GitKraken Desktop. See [Create a Task](/kepler/create-task).

---

---
# Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Settings has 15 pages, each with its own sections. These docs follow the rail's groups: one page for Setup and Account, one for each page of the work group, one for the app pages, one for the environment pages, and one for Updates and Help. Each describes what every setting controls, what it defaults to, and what changes when you change it. This page covers what the pages share.

Open Settings from the gear icon in the top bar, or with **⌘ ,** (**Ctrl ,** on Windows and Linux). The same shortcut closes Settings again, the way the gear button does.

***

## The Settings pages

The left rail starts with a **Search settings** field and [**Setup**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#setup), a progress ring that reopens the first-run checklist. Below them, the rail lists the pages in five unlabeled groups, separated by thin lines. The following table lists the pages in rail order:

| Page | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [**Account**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#account) | Who you're signed in as, your organization, what your plan unlocks, and GitKraken AI credits |
| [**Agents**](/kepler/settings-agents) | Your agents, custom agents, MCP servers, agent tools, approvals, and usage limits |
| [**Tasks**](/kepler/settings-tasks) | How new tasks start, including the default agent and the agent new sessions start with, and how a task's page looks |
| [**Repositories**](/kepler/settings-repositories) | The repositories folder, your repos and folders, worktrees and branches, and Projects |
| [**Integrations**](/kepler/settings-integrations) | Issue tracker and Git host connections, and sessions started in your own terminal |
| [**Actions**](/kepler/settings-actions) | Preferred Actions per item kind, and the Action list |
| [**General**](/kepler/settings-app#general) | Language, windows, the default editor, and keeping agents running |
| [**Notifications**](/kepler/settings-app#notifications) | Which agent events notify you, on the desktop and in Kepler |
| [**Appearance**](/kepler/settings-app#appearance) | Light or dark appearance and themes, the chat, the terminal font, code font size, and diff layout |
| [**Voice input**](/kepler/settings-app#voice-input) | On-device speech-to-text, its transcription engine, and learned words |
| [**Keyboard shortcuts**](/kepler/settings-app#keyboard-shortcuts) | Kepler's keyboard shortcuts |
| [**Remote environments**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-environments) | The machines your agents can run on, over SSH or WSL |
| [**Remote Access**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-access) | Opening this Kepler from another device |
| [**Updates**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#updates) | The installed version and app updates |
| [**Help**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#help) | The docs, release notes, onboarding guides, and Kepler's logs |

**Account** is first because it's the only page about the *person* rather than the app, and it's where the account menu hands off to.

### Find a setting

To find a setting by name, type in **Search settings**. Search matches section titles, control labels, help text, and common synonyms, so a word like *theme* or *notifications* finds the right section. With no match, the results read *No settings match "{query}"*.

Under the page you have open, the rail lists that page's main sections so you can jump to one. Under **Agents**, the rail also lists each supported agent below **Your agents**. A page with fewer than two listed sections shows no list.

### Sub-pages and unsaved changes

Item editors open as sub-pages inside their Settings page, with a breadcrumb back to the page. Examples include a repository, a project, a custom agent, an MCP server, and an Action.

If you leave a sub-page with unsaved changes, Kepler asks before it discards anything. It asks on every way out: **Escape**, **Back**, the form's own **Cancel**, a page in the Settings rail, or a link elsewhere in the app:

- A form that can save asks **Save your changes?**, with **Cancel**, **Don't save**, and **Save**.
- A form that has nothing to save yet, such as a step-by-step add flow, asks **Discard your changes?**, with **Keep editing** and **Discard**.

A form with a **Save** button keeps it in a footer with **Cancel**. While you have unsaved edits, the footer reads *Unsaved changes*. If a save fails, the footer shows why and keeps your edits on the form. A save that succeeds confirms with *Saved {name}*.

Most fields outside those forms save themselves. Each one shows its own status beside it: **Saving**, **Saved**, or **Unable to save** with the reason. A switch shows only **Saving** and a failure. If a save fails after you've left the page, Kepler tells you which setting it was: *Unable to save {label}*.

Moving between pages replaces a single history entry. As a result, **Back** returns you to whatever you were doing before you opened Settings, rather than walking back through every page you visited.

### Settings in a remote window

In a window connected to a remote environment, Settings shows that machine's settings, and its header names the machine. Each page states under its title where its settings are saved: **Saved on {machine}** or **Saved on this machine**. A section that saves somewhere other than its page carries its own badge. The **Saved on this machine** tooltip reads *Applies to every Kepler window on this machine, whichever machine it's connected to.* To change this machine's own settings from such a window, click **Open this machine's settings** in the header: it opens the same page in a local window.

### Deep links and section anchors

Every section has a stable anchor id. A link of the form `/settings/<page>#<section-id>` opens that page and scrolls to the section.

A bare `/settings` opens the last page that window had open, or **Agents** if there's none. Legacy links of the form `/settings#<section-id>` still work: Kepler resolves the id to the page that owns that section and keeps the hash. An id that no page owns anymore, such as `general`, `windows-and-notifications`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, or `features`, opens **Agents**.

The following table lists each page's path with its section anchors, in page order:

| Page path | Section anchors, in page order |
|---|---|
| `/settings/account` | `account`, `plan-features`, `ai-credits` |
| `/settings/agents` | `agents`, `custom-agents`, `mcp-servers`, `agent-git-tools`, `approvals`, `usage-limits` |
| `/settings/tasks` | `new-tasks`, `default-agent`, `task-page` |
| `/settings/repositories` | `repositories-root`, `repositories`, `worktrees`, `projects` |
| `/settings/integrations` | `provider-integrations`, `agent-options` |
| `/settings/actions` | `preferred-actions`, `action-list` |
| `/settings/general` | `language`, `windows`, `default-editor`, `keep-running` |
| `/settings/notifications` | `system-notifications` |
| `/settings/appearance` | `appearance`, `transcript`, `terminal`, `code`, `diff-view` |
| `/settings/voice` | `voice`, `voice-engine`, `voice-dictation`, `voice-learned` |
| `/settings/keyboard-shortcuts` | `shortcuts-general`, `shortcuts-navigation`, `shortcuts-dashboard`, `shortcuts-task-page`, `shortcuts-chat`, `shortcuts-changes` |
| `/settings/remote-environments` | `remote-environments`, `found-machines`, `remote-windows` |
| `/settings/remote-access` | `remote-access` |
| `/settings/updates` | `updates` |
| `/settings/help` | `onboarding-help`, `logs` |

`default-agent` sits inside **New tasks** rather than being a section of its own. From the rail or search, `worktrees` opens the **Worktrees and branches** sub-page instead of scrolling to its row. Each agent also gets its own anchor on the Agents page, `agent-<agent-id>`, for example `agent-claude-code`, and each custom agent gets `custom-agent-row-<id>`.

When search, or a pointer on another page, sends you to one setting, Kepler marks that setting as you arrive, then fades the mark, and moves focus to it.

---

---
# Setup and Account Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-setup-account/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

The first two entries of the Settings rail are about you rather than the app: **Setup** and **Account**.

## Setup

**Setup** sits at the top of the rail, under **Search settings**. Its progress ring shows how much of the first-run checklist is done, and clicking it reopens the checklist. For what the checklist asks you to do, and how to hide it from the toolbar, see [Getting Started → Finish the setup checklist](/kepler/kepler-getting-started#finish-the-setup-checklist).

***

## Account

The Account page has three sections: **Account**, **Unlock more with Kepler**, and **GitKraken AI credits**. The following table lists its controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Account** | Who you're signed in as, with your name and email |
| Organization | Your active organization and its plan. When your GitKraken account belongs to more than one organization, this line becomes a switcher. What a feature costs, and whether it's unlocked at all, follows the organization you're acting as |
| **Refresh account status** | Re-reads your plan. Kepler also picks up a purchase or plan change made outside the app on its own, with no restart |
| **Manage account** / **Manage subscription** | Opens your GitKraken account or subscription on gitkraken.dev |
| **Unlock more with Kepler** | What this plan does and doesn't include. Shown only while something is left to unlock |
| **GitKraken AI credits** | Your credit balance, with **Buy credits**, and **Your usage by feature**. Shown only when there's a balance to show |

**Your usage by feature** shows where your AI credits went. A stacked bar splits your use between your three most-used AI features and everything else as **Other**. Below the bar, each feature has a row with its share of your use as a percentage, such as **Commit Message**, **Conflict Resolution**, **Compose Changes**, or **Task & branch names**. Hover a feature's help icon for what it does. The breakdown appears only once you've used an AI feature.

When a feature is locked on the organization you're acting as but included on another one you belong to, Kepler says so and offers the switch rather than sending you to a paywall: *{organization} ({plan}) already includes this.*, with **Switch to organization**.

A paywall also asks **Already upgraded?** with **Check again**, for a plan you've just changed. If nothing has changed, it says so briefly: *Still on {plan}*. A paywall that covers the whole window also shows an account card: **Signed in as**, your **Current organization**, and a **Switch** button for each other organization whose plan includes the feature.

### Trials

When a trial starts, a dialog reads **You just opened up all of Kepler**, with a pill showing how many days are free (*{count} days free*). It lists what the trial unlocks: *Every feature below is yours until {date}.* When the trial ends, a dialog reads **Your trial has ended** and lists **What your trial included**. It offers an upgrade or, when your account can start the trial again, a way to pick up where you left off.

# Agent Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-agents/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

*The coding agents that work on your tasks: install them, sign in, choose how you work with each, and give them more tools.* The page opens with a line that names your default agent, *New tasks use {agent}.*, and a **Change in Tasks** link to [Default agent](/kepler/settings-tasks#default-agent).

The Agents page has six sections: **Your agents**, **Custom agents**, **MCP servers**, **Agent tools**, **Approvals**, and **Usage limits**.

## Your agents

Kepler ships adapters for **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **OpenCode**, **Pi**, **Auggie**, **Antigravity**, **Cursor**, and **Grok Build**. Settings lists the agents installed on this machine first, then the rest, each group in that order.

Two buttons sit in the section header: **Update all** runs each installed agent's own updater, and **Re-scan** re-detects the agent CLIs installed on this system. Run **Re-scan** after you install or remove an agent outside Kepler.

Each card's title line carries the agent's name and these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Version | The installed version. **Not installed** when Kepler can't find the CLI. A warning-toned **Version unknown** means Kepler was unable to read it, which turns off features that depend on the version, such as sending a new session's first message automatically. Reinstalling or updating the agent usually fixes it |
| **Update** | Runs the agent's updater and streams its output. Shown when Kepler has an updater for that agent |
| **Install** | Runs an install method on your behalf and streams the output. Shown on a not-installed agent that has an installer for your OS. **Cancel** stops an install in progress: *Install cancelled: {name}* |
| **Enabled** | *Off keeps it installed but hidden when you start work.* |

When the installed version of an agent, or of one of its components, is known to misbehave, a warning note sits on the card under the title line. The note names the version and says what to do. Kepler ships these notes:

| Note | What it means |
|---|---|
| *OpenCode {version} is not supported* | Sessions with this version won't start. Install OpenCode 2, or choose an OpenCode 2 binary under **Program and data folder** |
| *Auggie {version} may not load your MCP servers in chat* | Kepler's fix for how Auggie loads MCP servers covers only the Auggie versions it was built for |
| *ACP server {version} can fail to start on Linux* | Antigravity's Chat server can be killed at startup on some Linux systems. Reinstall it under **Program and data folder** |
| *Codex {version} can show approval prompts that need no answer* | Update Codex to 0.163.0 or newer |

The card body holds the rest:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Accounts** | Runs multiple logins side by side, each with its own credentials and history but sharing your skills, agents, commands, and settings. **Add account** asks whether its conversations **Keep separate** or **Share with the CLI**. Each account row has a color picker that tints the agent icon wherever that account runs (the default account stays uncolored, so its picker shows the ⊘ **No color** mark), plus **Sign in** and an account menu with **Rename**, **Share history with the CLI**, **Sign in another way**, **Sign out**, and **Remove account**. On a signed-in Claude Code account, the menu also has **Switch account…**, which signs that account in with a different Claude login (see below). Removing an account stops its running sessions and deletes the sessions stored only in it, unless you first **Move to CLI account**; see [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#several-accounts-for-one-agent). Available for Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Auggie, and Grok Build |
| **Account** | On an agent with a single login: who is signed in, with **Sign in** or **Sign out**. Signing out deletes the stored credentials |
| **New sessions start in** | The default mode for new sessions. See below |
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Program and data folder** | A disclosure holding **Binary**, **Components**, and **Data folder** |

Under **Program and data folder**:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Binary** | The binary Kepler spawns. **Auto** resolves it the way your shell does (the first match on your `PATH`), so it matches `which`. Pick a specific install, or **Custom path…**, to override. **Re-scan** searches again | Auto |
| **Components** | Extra pieces an agent can need, such as its CLI for Terminal mode (*Needed for Terminal mode.*), each with **Install** or **Update to {version}** | None |
| **Data folder** | *Overrides the agent's default data and config folder.* | Empty, meaning the agent's own default |

**Codex runs your own CLI.** Kepler resolves and spawns the `codex` you have installed, like every other agent. Usage figures read the OAuth token from `~/.codex/auth.json`, or `CODEX_HOME/auth.json` when you have set a custom data folder.

**OpenCode needs version 2.** Kepler reads and resumes only OpenCode 2's sessions, and a session won't start on an OpenCode 1 binary: the card shows *OpenCode {version} is not supported*. If you have both installed, point **Binary** at OpenCode 2. A conversation you started under OpenCode 1 resumes from OpenCode 2's copy of it. **Antigravity** runs in Chat through its ACP server, a separate component from its `agy` terminal CLI. See [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations).

### When an added account stops sharing your settings

An added account shares your own settings, instructions, skills, agents, commands, and other configuration by linking to your files. If the agent saves a change while signed in to that account, it can write its own copy in place of the link, and the account stops following your file. Kepler flags this under the account's row: *This account stopped sharing your {items}*. Expand it to see both paths, **This account's copy** and **Your {item}**, and choose one of the following:

- **Share your {item} again** asks first, then links the account back to your file. *Its own copy is saved as a backup next to it, so nothing is lost.*
- **Keep its own {item}** keeps the account's copy. The row's menu then offers **Share your {item} again** if you change your mind.

### Switch the account a Claude Code login uses

**Switch account…** opens **Switch the account for {name}?**, which names the login now signed in. *If your browser is already signed in, choose a different account on the sign-in page.* The dialog also warns you about the following:

- How many running sessions use the account, and when they pick up the new login: when they restart, or on their next request.
- On the default account, the one the CLI uses, the switch *also changes the account the claude command uses in your own terminals.*

**Continue** opens the usual sign-in. When it succeeds, Kepler confirms: *{name} is now signed in as {login}.*

### Default mode for new sessions

Every agent that can run both ways carries this setting:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **New sessions start in** | **Chat**: *{agent} built into Kepler, with replies, diffs and plans you can read, review and search.* **Terminal**: *{agent}'s own command-line app, with its commands, shortcuts and settings, just as you use it today.* | Chat. Google Antigravity starts on Terminal, because its Chat server signs in separately |

The choice is saved per agent, so one agent can default to Terminal while another stays on Chat. The help text reads *You can pick the other one when you start a session.*: a new session can start in the other mode without changing the setting. A terminal-only agent shows **Terminal** with no switch. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs).

### Artifacts in new sessions

The following setting is on Claude Code's card:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | *The Artifact tools let the agent publish pages and designs. They add about 12k tokens to the context of every session that has them. Each session can still turn them on or off from its session menu.* | Off |

A running Chat session has its own **Artifacts** switch in its agent settings. Turning it on restarts the session and resumes the conversation, after Kepler asks **Turn on Artifacts?**. Once a conversation has artifacts on, they stay on for it. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

### Let artifact comments start turns

The following setting is on Claude Code's card:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Anyone with edit access to an artifact a Chat session publishes can start a turn in that session by sending a comment to Claude. A reply is posted automatically | On |

Running sessions keep the value they started with. When you change it, the card lists the sessions still using the previous value, marking those that **Published an artifact** or have a **Turn in progress**, with **Restart all** and **Restart selected ({count})**. Restarting keeps each conversation. A turn in progress is interrupted, and a restarted session stops watching artifacts it published before.

## Custom agents

*Run an agent that isn't listed above by giving Kepler its command.* To add one, click **New custom agent** in the section header. To edit one, click its row. Either opens the agent as a sub-page with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The name Kepler shows for the agent |
| **Command** | The program to run, for example `/usr/local/bin/my-agent` or `my-agent` |
| **Args (one per line)** | Arguments passed to the command |
| **Environment variables (KEY=value, one per line)** | Environment for the command |
| **Runs in** | **Chat**: *Kepler's chat. Needs a program that speaks ACP (the Agent Client Protocol).* **Terminal**: *The command's own app, in a terminal.* |

Added agents appear with the built-in agents everywhere an agent can be picked. With none added, the section reads *No custom agents yet.*

Kepler encrypts environment values at rest and hides existing ones when you edit an agent. Leave a value empty (`KEY=`) to keep the stored secret, or type a new value to replace it.

**Save** waits until the agent is stored. If the save fails, the form stays open with the reason: *Unable to save {name}: {reason}*. **Delete** asks first, **Delete custom agent?**: it *Deletes {name} and the environment values stored with it.* and can't be undone.

## MCP servers

*Give your agents extra tools, like a database, a browser or your issue tracker.* This section shows each agent's own MCP server defaults, which every project inherits.

To see the servers an agent loads, pick it with **Agent**, and pick an account when that agent has more than one. Only agents that expose their MCP servers to Kepler are listed. In the list:

- Click a server to open its own page. There you can turn the server or a single tool off, sign in to a server that needs it, use **Also add to…** to copy the server to another agent, and **Remove server**.
- Click **Add server** in the section header to add one.

A server or tool you turn off here is off in every repository, unless a repository turns it back on for itself. A repository's own **MCP servers** section is on its [Edit repo](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository) page. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers).

Below the list, one more setting applies across every agent:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep the GitKraken MCP server installed in every agent** | *Gives every command-line agent Git tools and your issues and pull requests through GitKraken. Turn off to manage it yourself.* | On |

This setting is about the MCP clients on your machine. It differs from the workspace MCP server that Kepler attaches to every session it starts itself, which is always on and has no setting. That server's tools are named by what they act on, such as `task_get`, `session_start`, or `worktree_create`. They give the agent tools to:

- Read a task and its resources, find tasks, create a task, change its Progress stage, name, or hold, and archive it.
- Read, write, and delete the task's notes.
- Attach and detach issue, pull request, and URL links, and attach or detach files.
- List the agents, repositories, and folders in your workspace. An agent can name a repository by one of its [aliases](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository).
- Create, attach, detach, update, or delete one of the task's worktrees.
- List and read sessions, start a session with the agent it chooses, send follow-ups, rename or archive a session, and read the reports its own sessions send back.
- List pending approvals.
- Read and save themes. See [Theme](/kepler/settings-app#theme).
- Rebase, merge, and compose commits, when [Agent tools](#agent-tools) turns them on.

Every workspace tool runs without the agent's own permission prompt, in Chat and Terminal alike. Instead, an action that needs your say, such as deleting a worktree or changing another task, waits for you on an approval card. See [Approvals](#approvals), and [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) for the full list of tools.

## Agent tools

*Kepler's own tools your agents can call, starting with rebasing, merging and cleaning up commits.* The following table lists them:

| Setting | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **AI Sync** | *Lets agents rebase or merge your branch and resolve conflicts for you. Every change can be undone.* | Off |
| **AI Compose** | *Lets agents turn messy changes into clean, focused commits. Every change can be undone.* | Off |

**AI Sync** and **AI Compose** add their tools to the workspace MCP server. Both require a paid GitKraken subscription. On the Community plan, they show a lock: *Not available on the Community plan. Upgrade to unlock.* Turning either on confirms that *New agent sessions will pick up this change.* Sessions already running keep the tools they started with.

## Approvals

*Some actions your agents take wait for your approval. These rules approve them for you; anything not covered still asks.*

When an agent asks, through Kepler's workspace tools, to do something that needs your say, Kepler pins an approval card above that session's message box. Examples include deleting a worktree, sending a prompt to another session, or rewriting a branch. The card's **Approve** menu offers **Always approve** for that kind of action. Kepler doesn't offer it for actions that can lose work. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

Each rule you create this way is listed under **Always approved**. A rule's row says when and where you added it, *Added {date} from {session} on {task}.*, and how often it has run, *Used {count} times, last {when}.* or *Not used yet.* **Remove** deletes the rule, so that kind of action asks again. With no rules, the section reads *No rules yet. When an agent asks, choose Always approve on its request to stop being asked about actions like it.*

## Usage limits

Two settings handle your agent plans' usage limits:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Check plan usage with each agent's provider** | *Kepler asks each agent's provider for your plan usage, per-model limits and extra usage, using the agent's own sign-in. The sign-in goes nowhere else and is never changed. When off, Kepler shows only what agents report, and a message queued at a usage limit is sent automatically only if the agent says when the limit resets.* | On |
| **Resume after the usage limit resets** | When a turn is cut off by your account usage limit and nothing is queued, Kepler queues a "continue" message that is sent shortly after the limit resets | Off |

***
